paragraphs: §1 — The Christians' Aristotelian proof that God is jawhar

We have already related concerning them [the Christians] that they claim the Creator (al-Bārī), holy be His names, to be one jawhar — three aqānīm. So let us begin, prior to investigating them and refuting them on the aqānīm and the Trinity (tathlīth), by investigating their basis for predicating jawhariyya of Him. They are to be asked: What is the proof that the Creator is a jawhar, and what is the consideration that requires the meaning of jawhariyya of Him?

Their reply to this is to say: Because He subsists in Himself (qāʾim bi-nafsih), and everything that subsists in itself is, without question, a jawhar. Their basis here is the logical postulates (al-awḍāʿ al-manṭiqiyya) — since Logic is for them a foundational source in the derivation of truths — and the author of Logic [Aristotle] defined jawhar as that which subsists in itself, not requiring another for its subsistence. Thus, since this is the definition of jawhar, and since the definition is convertible with the defined — namely, that every jawhar subsists in itself, and everything subsisting in itself is a jawhar — and since the Creator subsists in Himself, it is established that He is a jawhar.

: The Christian theologians Q is engaging — Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī (d. 974) is the contemporary touchstone, but the argument was inherited from Greek-Christian philosophical theology via the Syriac-Arabic translation movement — used the Aristotelian Categories definition of jawhar / ousia (substance) as that which subsists in itself, applying it to the Father, Son, and Spirit as one substance in three hypostases (aqānīm). The convertibility of the definition with the defined (al-ḥadd yanʿakis ʿalā maḥdūdih) is the standard kalāmī formalism Q exploits in §2. Direct Christian-side parallel: Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī, Maqāla fī al-Tawḥīd (in Perier 1920 ed., Arabic l. 191-194) opens with precisely this thesis: innamā gharaḍunā fī hādhihi al-maqāla an nubayyina jawāz mā taʿtaqiduhu al-naṣārā an al-Bāriʾ jalla wa-taʿālā jawhar wāḥid dhū thalāth ṣifāt kull wāḥida minhā ghayr al-ukhrayayn fī al-maʿnā ("our aim in this treatise is to demonstrate the admissibility of what the Christians believe: that the Creator is one substance with three attributes, each of them distinct in meaning from the other two"). Note that Yaḥyā softens aqānīm → ṣifāt (attributes), narrowing the gap to Bahshamī attribute-theology — a softening that Q targets in M3 B3 §5 by aligning the Christian and Ibn-Kullāb evasions. See [[glossary]] s.v. ṣifa.
§2 — The reductio: every jawhar is also receptive of opposites (i.e., accidents)

They are to be told: If Logic is a foundation to be relied upon, a base upon which to build, and a ladder for the derivation of truths — then its author [Aristotle], when defining jawhar, did not confine the definition to what you have mentioned. Rather, he added another clause: namely, that the jawhar is receptive of opposites in its essence (qābilun li-l-mutaḍāddāt fī dhātih).

So if you require for the Creator — exalted be His name — the meaning of jawhariyya on the ground that He subsists in Himself, then likewise require of Him the reception of opposites in His essence, since He is, on your account, a jawhar — and every jawhar is receptive of opposites, just as every receptive-of-opposites is a jawhar, by the conversion of the definition and the defined.

For this is what you have claimed on the basis of the logical postulates: that since the definition of jawhar is "that which subsists in itself," and since every subsisting-in-itself is a jawhar just as every jawhar subsists in itself — therefore likewise, since every receptive-of-accidents (qābilun li-l-aʿrāḍ) is a jawhar, it must be the case that every jawhar is receptive of accidents. If, however, the Creator (mighty and exalted) is a jawhar yet the definition of jawhar — viz. reception of accidents — does not bind Him, then why may He not be subsisting-in-Himself yet not be a jawhar, even though every subsisting-in-itself is [otherwise] a jawhar? They have no escape from this and can produce no distinction in it. Even if there were nothing against them beyond this argument, it would suffice as a conviction.

: This is Aristotle, Categories 4a-4b — the third idion of substance, that it is the same in number but receptive of contraries (e.g., the same body becomes pale and dark, the same man is now warm now cold). Q's deployment here is a clean katastrophē: the Aristotelian definition the Christians invoke convicts them, since by the same Aristotelian apparatus they must concede that whatever is a substance is receptive of accidents — incompatible with their own theology of the unchanging Creator. The parallel Bahshamī move is most cleanly preserved in ʿAbd al-Jabbār's Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa (= SUK) at l. 5392-5399 (under the heading sharḥ al-tathlīth wa-l-radd ʿalayhi): qawlukum innahu taʿālā jawhar wāḥid thalāthat aqānīm munāqaḍa ẓāhira, li-anna qawlanā fī al-shayʾ innahu wāḥid yaqtaḍī annahu fī al-wajh alladhī ṣāra wāḥidan lā yatajazzaʾ wa-lā yatabaʿʿaḍ, wa-qawlanā thalātha yaqtaḍī annahu mutajazzī… ("your saying that He is one substance and three hypostases is a manifest contradiction, since 'one' requires that He be indivisible in the respect in which He is one, while 'three' requires that He be divisible"). The contradiction-charge that Q develops via Aristotelian-receptive-of-opposites in B2 §2 is the same one SUK develops via the bare arithmetic of identity. Both presuppose the katastrophē against the Christian appeal to the Categories-tradition.
§3 — They have already in fact attached all nine accidents to Him
§3. Moreover, in their statement that He does not admit reception of accidents,
[p311] they are liars and self-contradictors — for in what they claim of the three aqānīm they have in fact attached the nine accidents to Him. Namely:

- When they say that He is three aqānīm, they have placed Him under number, which is quantity (kammiyya). - When they make Him living by a life and knowing by a knowledge, they have predicated of Him the attribute (ṣifa) — which is quality (kayfiyya). - When they call Him Father and Son, they have brought Him under relation (al-muḍāf).
These are the three simple accidents that they have attached to Him. As for the other six composite accidents, they have attached them to the Son — who is one of the aqānīm. Namely:

- They claim that Jesus, who is the Son, appeared at such-and-such a time, and was born in such-and-such a moment — they thus placed Him under time (matā, "when"). - They claim that He was in such-and-such a land, thus predicating existence in place of Him — which is the meaning of ayna ("where"). - They claim that He was clothed and rode — they thus required of Him possession / having (al-qunya). - They say that He sat and stood and walked — that is posture (al-niṣba). - They mention that He ate, drank, struck, took, gave — that is action (al-fiʿl). - And finally, that He was killed and crucified — that is passion and being-acted-upon (al-infiʿāl / al-mafʿūl).
What accident, then, remains among the [Aristotelian] accidents that they have not attached to Him and ascribed His reception of it?

: Q is running the nine accidents of the Aristotelian Categories (quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, having, action, affection) and showing the Trinity + Incarnation imply God has all of them — the very thing the Christians began by denying. The argument is structurally identical to one in ʿAbd al-Jabbār, Mughnī Vol. 5 (per the anchor grid). It is the philosophical pillar of medieval Jewish and Muslim anti-Christology.
§4 — Their argument for the hypostases (every agent → distinct life and knowledge)
Then we ask them about the aqānīm which on their view are: Knowledge (which is for them the Son), and Life (which for them is the Spirit). They are to be asked: What is your proof of this?

Their reply is to say: Every agent (fāʿil) must necessarily be living by a life (ḥayyan bi-ḥayāh) which is other than him, and knowing by a knowledge (ʿāliman bi-ʿilm) which is other than him. So when it is established that the Creator is an agent, it must follow that He is living by a life and knowing by a knowledge — and these, His knowledge and His life, are [two] aqānīm; and the jawhar is the third uqnūm. Then, since knowledge is generated from the knower as the son is generated from the father (tawallud al-ibn min al-ab), knowledge is for Him a Son; and since life only comes about by means of spirit (rūḥ), His life is for Him a Spirit. From all this it follows that He is three aqānīm: a Father — namely, the jawhar; a knowledge — namely, the Son; and a Spirit — namely, the Life.
§5 — Reductio: by your inference, God must also be a body with limbs

We answer them: In this proof of yours, you have likewise rested upon the observed, sensible agent (al-fāʿil al-mushāhad al-maḥsūs). Now if this is so — and the Creator must on that basis be living by a life and knowing by a knowledge,

[p310] because every observed agent is on this footing — then say also: since every observed agent is a body possessing limbs and instruments (jism dhū jawāriḥ wa-ālāt), it must follow that the Creator is a body, since He is an agent. And if it is admissible that the Creator be an agent yet not a body, nor possessing limbs and instruments, contrary to the observed — why then is it not admissible that He be an acting, living, knowing one by Himself (bi-dhātih), with no distinct knowledge and no distinct life there, contrary to the observed? There is no [valid] distinction.

Likewise it follows for them that He must be a body that is neither long, nor broad, nor deep — even though among observed beings there is no body free of those dimensions — just as [they say] He is a jawhar not receptive of accidents, even though every observed jawhar is receptive of accidents. There is no distinction.

The same reductio binds them in their statement that He is living. To wit: if the Creator is living by a life that is other than Him — because among observed beings there is no living thing except on this footing — then likewise He must be perceiving and moving (ḥassās mutaḥarrik), since among observed beings there is no living thing that is not perceiving and moving. And there is no distinction. If, however, the Creator is living but not perceiving and not moving, contrary to the observed — then likewise He is living not by a life, contrary to the observed. There is no distinction.
§6 — Dialectical questions about the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit

They are further questioned. We say to them: Tell us about the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. When you say He is one in essence (wāḥid fī l-maʿnā), do you say that the Father is the Son, and is also the Spirit?

If they answer: "He is not the Son and is not the Spirit" — we say to them: Then what objection do you have to the claim that the three are not one in essence — since none of the three is, individually, the three [taken together] in essence?
We further say to them: Tell us, is it admissible that there be three — Father, Son, and Spirit — and yet one in essence?
If they say "Yes," we say to them: Then what objection do you have to the claim that two — one pre-eternal (qadīm) and one temporally-originated (muḥdath) — are one in essence?

If they say "That is admissible," we say: Then what objection do you have to the claim that the pre-eternal is the temporally-originated, and the temporally-originated is the pre-eternal — and that the pre-eternal originated itself — since the temporally-originated is the pre-eternal, and the pre-eternal is the temporally-originated?

If they say: "It is not admissible that the pre-eternal and the temporally-originated be two in number and one in essence" — we say: Then in the same way, the Father and the Son and the Spirit cannot be three in number and one in essence.

: The qadīm / muḥdath dichotomy as a stress-test on Trinitarian identity is a Bahshamī commonplace, but Q's specific deployment — "if the three could be one in essence, then a pre-eternal and a temporally-originated could be one in essence" — has a near-exact parallel in SUK 5400-5404 (in the same radd ʿalā al-naṣārā section as the SUK 5392-5399 contradiction-charge cited in ): fa-law jāza fī Allāh taʿālā an yuqāl innahu jawhar wāḥid thalāthat aqānīm, la-jāza an yuqāl innahu qādir wāḥid thalāthat qādirīn, wa-ʿālim wāḥid thalāthat ʿālimīn, wa-ḥayy wāḥid thalāthat aḥyāʾ ("if it were admissible for God to be one substance and three hypostases, it would be admissible to say He is one qādir and three qādirūn, one ʿālim and three ʿālimūn, one ḥayy and three aḥyāʾ"). The argument-form is identical: any-N-things-cannot-be-one-in-essence iterated across the ṣifāt.
§7 — A further dialectical question on the Word (kalima / Logos)

Furthermore, we say to them: Since you say the Creator is living by life and speaking by speech (ḥayy bi-ḥayāh wa-nāṭiq bi-nuṭq) — for knowledge for them is identical with speech — tell us concerning His life: is it pre-eternal? If they say "Yes," we say: Then you must hold that the Life is living and speaking, and that the Speech (nuṭq) is living and speaking. If they say "Yes," we say: Then what objection do you have to the claim that each one of these three [the Father, Life/Spirit, Knowledge/Word] is itself three? — since the Father had to have a Son and a Spirit alongside Him because He is living and speaking; the same must apply to the Spirit. If they say "The Spirit is not living and not speaking, and likewise the Speech [is not living and not speaking]" — we say to them: Then tell us about the Speech: do you say that it is an agent, a Maker? If they say "Speech is neither agent nor Maker" — we say to them: Then what objection… [text breaks; argument continues into bab 3 on the eternity of the Word].

: Al-nuṭq (rational speech / logos) and al-ʿilm (knowledge) here function as near-synonyms — both render the divine Logos of Christian theology. This sets up the move to Bab 3, where Q targets the doctrine of qidam al-kalima (the eternity of the Word) — the same conceptual apparatus the Bahshamīs deployed against the Muslim doctrine of the uncreated Qurʾān (qidam al-Qurʾān), now redirected at the Christological Logos.

- The Aristotelian jawhar-trap (§§1-2): Q's central move is to take the Christian appeal to al-awḍāʿ al-manṭiqiyya — the Aristotelian Categories tradition transmitted through the Baghdad school (Mattā b. Yūnus, Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī, Fārābī) — and force them to take the whole of the Aristotelian definition. Since "jawhar = that-which-subsists-in-itself" was the convenient half they appealed to, Q insists they accept the second clause too: "jawhar = that-which-is-receptive-of-opposites" (i.e., susceptible to accidents). Either God is a jawhar in the full Aristotelian sense (and hence subject to accidents — incoherent with their own theology of divine simplicity), or He is not a jawhar — in which case their argument for the aqānīm loses its starting point.

- The nine-accidents catalogue (§3): Q runs through the standard kalāmī formalization of Aristotle's nine accidents (omitting jawhar / substance itself, since that is the tenth category) and shows the Christians have predicated all of them of God: three (quantity, quality, relation) via the Trinity formula and six (place, time, having, posture, action, affection) via the Incarnation. The full nine-accidents inventory is a kalāmī commonplace by Q's time; cf. Saadia, Amānāt II.

- "tawallud al-ibn min al-ab" (§4): The technical term Christian theologians used for the Son's eternal generation from the Father — Q renders the Christian gennēsis / ولادة الابن من الآب into kalāmī vocabulary in order to reduce it to the same generative-causation apparatus he is about to demolish.

- The "observed agent" reductio (§5): Classic kalāmī qiyās ghāʾib ʿalā shāhid (analogy from the unseen to the visible) — but used here in destructive mode: Q grants the Christian inference-pattern (every observed agent is living-by-life-other-than-itself → so God) and shows it leads, by parity of reasoning, to also: every observed agent is a body with limbs → so God. The Christians cannot accept that conclusion, so they must reject the inference-pattern itself — and with it their argument for the aqānīm.

- §6 unity-and-multiplicity dilemmas: Q deploys the standard kalāmī "qadīm / muḥdath" dichotomy as a stress test. If "three in number can be one in essence," then a pre-eternal and a temporally-originated could also be one in essence — leading to the absurdity that the qadīm originated itself. This is the same family of arguments deployed by Bahshamī polemicists (and inherited from Greek anti-Christian polemic via the Mughnī) against Christology.

- The transition to Bab 3 (the eternity of the Word): §7's question about whether divine speech is itself "living and speaking" leads into the qidam al-kalima discussion of Bab 3. As Q will argue there, the Bahshamī apparatus deployed against the Muslim doctrine of the uncreated Qurʾān works equally well against the Christian doctrine of the eternal Word — a "methodologically subversive" parallel in the anchor-grid scheme: Q uses the Bahshamī apparatus on a target the Bahshamīs would have shared.
